name: Non-incisional double eyelid (suture method)

card.summary: Buried-suture double eyelid surgery creates a crease with stitches instead of an incision; popular in Asia, with literature focused on crease loss and suture complications.
card.aka: Buried suture double eyelid, suture method, stitch double eyelid
card.note: Crease loss, reoperation and suture-related eye complications are documented.

quick.overview:
The suture method forms an upper-lid crease by passing buried stitches through the lid so that skin is tethered to deeper tissue, without a skin incision. It is described as very popular in Asia, especially China.

Studies are retrospective and focus on how long creases last and on complications. Surgeons contrast it with the incision method, which involves a skin cut.
quick.mechanism: Sutures are placed through the eyelid at one or more points (for example two-point or continuous techniques) and buried, creating an adhesion that forms the crease line.
quick.risks: Reports describe suture exposure causing corneal damage, sometimes initially misdiagnosed, crease loss from suture loosening and reoperation, and suture-related complications needing removal.

lead: Non-incisional (buried suture) double eyelid surgery creates an upper-lid crease by placing stitches through the lid rather than cutting skin. Surgical papers describe it as one of two alternative approaches, the other being the incision method, and as very popular in Asia, especially China.[1][2][3]

Because it implants suture thread, authors say foreign-material complications must be considered.[3] Recent literature examines crease loss, reoperation risk by age and fat removal, and eyebrow position changes.[6][7][8][9][10]
The studies located are retrospective cohorts and case series.

paras: Variants in the literature include two-point buried suture,[10] continuous buried suture,[7] hidden non-incisional suture,[6] and orbicularis-levator-tarsus fixation suturing.[5] Two modified techniques were proposed to reduce complications specific to buried sutures.[3]

The HIROSHIMA Study, a high-volume retrospective observational study, used multivariate analysis to examine crease loss after hidden non-incisional suture surgery.[6] Other retrospective cohorts compared one-year outcomes in 788 cases between younger and older patients,[7] examined reoperation after upper eyelid fat removal over 4.5 years,[9] and analysed age-related reoperation risk from suture loosening.[10]

A Japanese series of 210 upper lids described suture-related complications and compared removal techniques.[1] Chinese series report corneal injury and conjunctival complications from exposed sutures, with one 14-patient study describing misdiagnosis before correct identification.[2][4]
A 2026 report examined eyebrow position changes after double eyelid surgery in relation to preoperative compensatory brow elevation.[8]

Evidence found is retrospective: complication series,[1][2][3][4] and recent cohort analyses of durability and reoperation.[6][7][9][10] No randomised comparison of suture and incision methods was found in the sources reviewed.
